summary: Specifies a standard way to carry IP and ARP datagrams over ARCNET networks. It is now historic and was replaced by RFC 1201.

eli5.summary: ARCNET was one kind of local computer network. This memo explains how to wrap Internet packets so they ride on it.

questions: how to send ip over arcnet
subtitle: Wrapping Internet packets to send them over ARCNET local area networks.

tldr.problem: ARCNET local area networks could not carry IP datagrams in standard form because they had different frame formats and addressing schemes.
tldr.mechanism: IP and ARP packets are wrapped in ARCNET frames with specific system codes (240 for IP, 241 for ARP), with the ARCNET network handling address mapping between 32-bit IP addresses and 8-bit ARCNET node IDs.
tldr.outcome: This standard enabled IP networks over ARCNET, but ARCNET became obsolete and the RFC was replaced by RFC 1201.

today: RFC 1051 is historic and was replaced by RFC 1201. ARCNET is rarely used today, making this standard largely obsolete.

sections.title: ARCNET and IP
sections.content: ARCNET was a local area network technology with different addressing and frame formats than IP. RFC 1051 specifies how to encapsulate IP and ARP datagrams inside ARCNET packet frames so the two can work together.
sections.eli5: ARCNET and Internet packets speak different languages. This explains how to translate between them.

sections.title: Frame Format and System Codes
sections.content: ARCNET frames have a system code field that identifies the payload type. For IP, the system code is 240; for ARP, it is 241. ARCNET supports two packet formats: normal packets with 1 to 253 octets of data and extended packets with 257 to 508 octets. A forbidden range of 254-256 octets exists, so IP packets in that range must be padded with zeros to at least 257 octets.
sections.eli5: ARCNET labels each packet with a number saying what kind of data it holds. IP uses label 240, and ARP uses 241.

sections.title: Address Mapping
sections.content: IP addresses must be mapped to ARCNET's 8-bit node IDs. Two methods are recommended: extracting the low 8 bits of the IP host number, or using Address Resolution Protocol to look up mappings dynamically. ARP is optional but useful when IP implementations do not support subnetting. The broadcast address maps to ARCNET node ID 0.
sections.eli5: IP addresses and ARCNET addresses are different sizes. Implementers can use the simple method of taking the last 8 bits, or ask the network to look up the right address.

references.text: Plummer, D., "An Ethernet Address Resolution Protocol", RFC 826, November 1982.
